q: The limit is 100 requests a minute. You run 4 servers, and each one counts in its own memory. The load balancer spreads 400 requests evenly. How many get in, and what is the fix?
options: 100, because the limit is 100
25, because each server sees 100 and shares the limit
400, because each server counts 100 and allows them all. Keep one shared count in Redis
200, because the load balancer drops half of them. Add a bigger limit
why: Each server only sees its own 100 requests, so the real limit is 100 times 4. A request can land on any server, so the count must live in one shared place: Redis, changed in one step.

q: Two servers check the same client at once. The client has used 2 of 3. Each server reads the count, sees 2, then writes 3 and allows. What is the problem, and how does Redis INCR fix it?
options: 4 requests got in but the count says 3. INCR adds 1 and returns the new number in one step, so one gets 3 and the other gets 4
The count went down to 1. INCR makes Redis count slower
Both requests are refused. INCR makes Redis allow more
The key expired. INCR gives the key a longer end time
why: This is the same check-then-save race as the alias in the shortener. Never read, decide, then write. Redis runs one command at a time, so with INCR one server gets 3 (allowed) and the other gets 4 (429).

q: A fixed window allows 3 requests per clock minute. A client sends 3 at 12:00:59 and 3 more at 12:01:01. What happens, and which ways do not have this problem?
options: The last 3 are refused. All limiters behave like this
All 6 are allowed within 2 seconds, twice the limit, because the count goes back to 0 at the new minute. A sliding window or a token bucket avoids this
All 6 are refused because the client was too fast
Only 1 is allowed. A fixed window is always strict
why: This is the edge problem of a fixed window. A sliding window still counts most of last minute at 12:01:01. A token bucket has no clock edge: tokens drip in slowly, so after a burst the client has to wait.

q: A mobile app opens and sends 10 calls at once, then goes quiet. Which counting way fits this normal behaviour best?
options: A fixed window with a limit of 1 a minute
A token bucket, because the bucket size sets the biggest burst and the drip speed sets the average
A sliding window with a limit of 1 a second
No limit, because bursts are always safe
why: A token bucket allows a burst on purpose, up to the bucket size, and then makes the client wait while tokens drip back. It is the default for most API routes. A sliding window is better for strict, small limits like login.

q: A token bucket holds 3 tokens and gains 1 a second. It is empty at 1,500 ms, and a request comes at 1,600 ms. Is there a timer that adds tokens, and what happens to that request?
options: A timer adds a token every second, so the request is allowed
No timer. Each request adds the tokens for the time that passed. Only 0.1 token grew back, so it is refused
The bucket is refilled to 3 at once after 1 second, so the request is allowed
The request waits in a line until a token arrives
why: No timer is needed. On each request the code adds the tokens for the time that passed, up to the cap, so each client needs only two numbers: the tokens and the last time. With less than 1 token, the answer is 429 with a Retry-After.

q: Redis is down. What should the limiter do on the products route, and on the OTP login route?
options: Fail closed on both, to be safe
Fail open on both, so no user is blocked
Fail closed on products and open on OTP
Fail open on products and alert loudly. Fail closed on OTP, because each OTP message costs money and bots target it
why: A broken limiter should not take the whole app down, so most routes fail open. Login, OTP and money routes fail closed, because there the limiter protects accounts and money. Give the Redis call a short timeout so a slow Redis acts like a down one.
